title: Gastroesophageal Junction and Pylorus Distensibility Before and After Sleeve Gastrectomy—pilot Study with EndoFlipTM
question: Does sleeve gastrectomy change how easily the gastroesophageal junction and the pylorus distend on EndoFlip, and does the junction measurement before surgery relate to reflux a year later?

bottom_line.question: Does sleeve gastrectomy change how easily the gastroesophageal junction and the pylorus distend on EndoFlip, and does the junction measurement before surgery relate to reflux a year later?
bottom_line.answer: In nine patients, the distensibility index of the gastroesophageal junction at 40 ml filling rose from 1.4 to 2.9 mm2/mmHg a year after sleeve gastrectomy (p=0.046); this is a pilot result that the authors say needs confirming in larger studies.

provenance.quote: EndoFlipTM at 40 ml the DI of the GEJ was significantly higher post-SG compared to the presurgical assessment (1.4 mm2/mmHg [1.1-2.6] vs. 2.9 mm2/mmHg [2.6–5.3], p value=0.046)

sections.title: Why Reflux After Sleeve Gastrectomy Matters
sections.markdown: Sleeve gastrectomy is a weight-loss operation that removes most of the stomach. Its main drawback is reflux. Some patients develop gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) for the first time after surgery, and others find that existing reflux gets worse. GERD lowers quality of life and raises the risk of long-term complications. Much of it depends on the **gastroesophageal junction** (GEJ), the valve-like zone where the esophagus meets the stomach, also called the lower esophageal sphincter.

sections.title: Measuring How Easily the Valves Open
sections.markdown: The researchers used EndoFlip, a balloon probe placed during endoscopy that measures how easily a sphincter stretches open. It reports a **distensibility index** (DI) in square millimetres of opening per mmHg of pressure. A higher DI means a looser sphincter that opens more easily. The team predicted that the operation would raise the DI at both the GEJ and the pylorus, the valve at the stomach's outlet.

sections.title: Who Was Studied and How
sections.markdown:
This pilot study followed nine adults with severe obesity at a Swiss university hospital. Each had EndoFlip measurements before surgery, during it and one year later, plus endoscopy, pressure testing of the esophagus and acid monitoring. A patient counted as having GERD if both of these held:

acid exposure time above 6% and more than 80 reflux episodes

sections.title: Key Results
sections.markdown:
Results, with the balloon filled to 40 ml:

- GEJ DI roughly doubled after surgery, from 1.4 to 2.9 mm2/mmHg (p = 0.046).
- Pylorus DI rose from 6.0 to 13.1 mm2/mmHg (p = 0.046).
- Seven patients had usable reflux data. The four with reflux one year after surgery had a looser GEJ before surgery than the three without (2.6 vs 0.5 mm2/mmHg, p = 0.031).
- Weight loss did not differ between the reflux and no-reflux groups. Measurements taken during surgery and at one year did not separate the two groups either.

sections.title: What It Means and Its Limits
sections.markdown: According to the authors, a pre-surgery EndoFlip reading might identify patients likely to develop reflux after the operation. They suggest the looser pylorus may be linked to faster stomach emptying. That finding disagrees with an earlier study by Desprez and colleagues, which did not see the pylorus loosen. With only nine patients, the study was too small to support firm predictions. EndoFlip also has no established normal values yet, so the result needs confirming in larger studies.

sources.Sec1/p1: A major drawback of sleeve gastrectomy (SG) is the postoperative development of “de novo” or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) [–]. GERD is considered a risk factor for long-term complications and decreases the quality of life [–]. The gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) (often also referred to as the lower esophageal sphincter) plays an essential role in the complex pathophysiology of GERD, and a better understanding of the associated anatomical and functions is necessary. To date, the usefulness of an endoscopic functional luminal imaging probe (EndoFlip™) in bariatric patients before and after SG to assess the pathophysiological changes in the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and pylorus with regard to GERD is poorly described. We hypothesized that SG leads to increased distensibility indices (DI) of the GEJ and the pylorus.
sources.Sec2/p1: This prospective diagnostic observational study included patients (informed consent, ≥18 years, BMI ≥35 kg/m2, fulfillment of the Swiss Society for the Study of morbid obesity and metabolic disorders guidelines criteria) undergoing elective SG at a tertiary care university hospital. The study was approved by the local ethics committee (BASEC ID 2017-00923). Exclusion criteria were pregnancy or breastfeeding, oral anticoagulant, known bleeding disorder, and contraindication for endoscopic examination. Patients underwent esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD), pH-impedance monitoring, high-resolution manometry, and EndoFlip™ (Crospon Medical Devices, Galway, Ireland). GERD was defined (Lyon Consensus 2018) as distal oesophageal acid (pH<4) exposure time >6% and a total number of reflux episodes >80 (as per pH-impedance monitoring) [] and was differentiated between no, stable, de novo, or resolved status when comparing pre and postoperative data. Bariatric outcomes were reported in accordance with the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) guidelines []. Statistical analysis (categorical by Pearson chi-square test and continuous by Mann–Whitney U test) was performed using SPSS Statistics version 25 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York).
